content: 1. Exposure to one or more contaminated media can lead to health risks depending on the type and level of contamination. 2. A facultative pond is an aerobic pond designed to degrade organic matter and inactivate pathogens. It is typically the second type of pond in a waste stabilization pond system. 3. Faecal sludge refers to sludges of varying consistency collected from on-site sanitation systems, such as latrines, non-sewered public toilets, septic tanks, and aqua privies. This term also includes septage, which is faecal sludge specifically collected from septic tanks. 4. Flocculation is the process of agglomerating colloidal and finely divided suspended matter after coagulation. This is achieved through gentle stirring, either mechanically or hydraulically. 5. The geometric mean is a measure of central tendency that differs from the arithmetic mean by using multiplication rather than addition to summarize data values. It is particularly useful when data changes occur in a relative manner. 6. Greywater is water originating from kitchens, baths, and laundry activities. It generally does not contain significant concentrations of excreta. 7. Groundwater refers to water stored in rocks or subsoil layers. 8. A grow-out pond is a pond used to raise adult fish from fingerlings. 9. A hazard is any biological, chemical, physical, or radiological agent with the potential to cause harm. 10. A health-based target is a defined level of health protection for a specific exposure, such as 10^-6 DALY per person per year or the absence of a particular disease related to that exposure. 11. Health impact assessment involves estimating the effects of specific actions, such as plans, policies, or programs, on the health of a defined population in a given environment. 12. High-rate treatment processes are engineered systems characterized by high flow rates and low hydraulic retention times. These typically include a primary treatment step to settle solids, followed by a secondary treatment step to biodegrade organic substances. 13. Hydraulic retention time refers to the time wastewater takes to pass through a treatment system. 14. Hypochlorite, such as sodium or calcium hypochlorite, is a chemical commonly used for disinfection. 15. Indicator organisms are microorganisms whose presence indicates faecal contamination and potentially the presence of more harmful microorganisms. 16. Infection occurs when an infectious agent enters, develops, or multiplies within a host. This can be evidenced by symptoms (e.g., diarrhea) or the presence of antibodies against the agent. 17. Legislation refers to laws enacted by a legislative body or the act of creating and enacting laws. 18. Localized irrigation involves applying water directly to crops using technologies like drip or bubbler irrigation. This method generally uses less water, reduces crop contamination, and minimizes human contact with wastewater. 19. Low-rate biological treatment systems use biological processes to treat wastewater in large basins, often earthen ponds. These systems are characterized by long hydraulic retention times and include examples like waste stabilization ponds, wastewater storage and treatment reservoirs, and constructed wetlands. 20. A maturation pond is an aerobic pond with algal growth and high levels of bacterial removal. It is usually the final type of pond in a waste stabilization pond system. 21. The median is the middle value in a data series, where 50% of the values are lower and 50% are higher than the median. 22. Membrane filtration is a technique that uses a physical barrier (a membrane) with specific pore sizes to trap contaminants larger than the pore size on the membrane's surface. Smaller contaminants may pass through or be captured within the membrane by other mechanisms. 23. Metacercariae are the infective life cycle stage of trematode parasites that can infect humans. These can form cysts in fish muscle tissue or on plant surfaces, depending on the trematode species. 24. Multiple barriers refer to the use of more than one preventive measure to protect against hazards. 25. Off-site sanitation systems involve the removal of excreta from the plot occupied by a dwelling and its immediate surroundings. 26. On-site sanitation systems store excreta within the plot occupied by a dwelling and its immediate surroundings. Treatment of faecal matter may occur on-site through extended in-pit consolidation and storage or require off-site collection and treatment. 27. Oocysts are the infectious and environmental stage of certain protozoa, such as Cryptosporidium, resulting from sexual reproduction during their life cycle. For enteric protozoa, oocysts are excreted in faeces. 28. Operational monitoring focuses on parameters that can be measured quickly and easily to determine if a process is functioning properly. This data helps managers make corrections to prevent hazard breakthroughs. 29. An overhanging latrine is a type of latrine that empties directly into a pond or other water body. 30. pH is a measure of the intensity of the acidic or basic condition of a liquid. 31. Policy refers to a set of procedures, rules, and allocation mechanisms that provide the basis for programs and services. Policies set priorities and allocate resources for implementation through instruments like laws, regulations, economic measures, and education programs. 32. Primary treatment is the initial process in wastewater treatment, designed to remove settleable organic and inorganic solids through sedimentation and floating substances (scum) by skimming. Examples include primary sedimentation, chemically enhanced sedimentation, and upflow anaerobic sludge blanket reactors. 33. Quantitative microbial risk assessment (QMRA) is a method for assessing risks from specific hazards through different exposure pathways. It includes four components: hazard identification, exposure assessment, dose-response assessment, and risk characterization. 34. Regulations are rules created by an administrative agency to interpret statutes that define the agency's purpose and powers or the circumstances of applying the statute. 35. Restricted irrigation involves using wastewater to grow crops that are not consumed raw by humans. 36. Risk is the likelihood of a hazard causing harm in exposed populations within a specified timeframe, including the magnitude of that harm. 37. Risk assessment is the process of using available information to predict the likelihood and magnitude of hazards or specified events. 38. Risk management involves systematically evaluating wastewater, excreta, or greywater use systems, identifying hazards and hazardous events, assessing risks, and developing and implementing preventive strategies to manage those risks. 39. Secondary treatment is the wastewater treatment step following primary treatment. It removes biodegradable dissolved and colloidal organic matter using high-rate, engineered aerobic biological processes. Examples include activated sludge, trickling filters, aerated lagoons, and oxidation ditches. 40. Septage refers to sludge removed from septic tanks. 41. A septic tank is an underground tank that treats wastewater through solids settling and anaerobic digestion. Effluents may be discharged into soak pits or small-bore sewers. 42. Sewage is a mixture of human excreta and water used to flush excreta from toilets through pipes. It may also contain water used for domestic purposes. 43. A sewer is a pipe or conduit that carries wastewater or drainage water. 44. Sewerage is a complete system of pipes, pumps, basins, tanks, unit processes, and infrastructure for collecting, transporting, treating, and discharging wastewater. 45. Sludge is a mixture of solids and water that settles at the bottom of latrines, septic tanks, and ponds or is produced as a by-product of wastewater treatment. 46. Source separation involves diverting urine, faeces, greywater, or all of these, followed by separate collection and treatment. 47. Thermotolerant coliforms are a group of bacteria whose presence in the environment usually indicates faecal contamination. They were previously referred to as faecal coliforms. 48. Tolerable daily intake (TDI) is the amount of a toxic substance that can be ingested daily over a lifetime without exceeding a certain level of risk. 49. Tolerable health risk is a defined level of health risk from a specific exposure or disease that is considered acceptable by society. It is used to set health-based targets. 50. Turbidity refers to the cloudiness of water caused by the presence of fine suspended matter. 51. Ultraviolet (UV) radiation consists of light waves shorter than visible blue-violet waves (ranging from 380 to 10 nanometres) and is used for pathogen inactivation, including bacteria, protozoa, and viruses. 52. Unrestricted irrigation involves using treated wastewater to grow crops that are typically consumed raw. 53. An upflow anaerobic sludge blanket reactor is a high-rate anaerobic unit used for the primary treatment of domestic wastewater. Wastewater is treated as it passes through a sludge layer composed of anaerobic bacteria, primarily for the removal of organic matter. 54. Waste-fed aquaculture involves using wastewater, excreta, and/or greywater as inputs to aquacultural systems. 55. Waste stabilization pond treatment systems typically consist of anaerobic, facultative, and maturation ponds linked in series. 56. Wastewater is liquid waste discharged from homes, commercial premises, and similar sources into individual disposal systems or municipal sewer pipes. It mainly contains human excreta and used water. Domestic or municipal wastewater does not include industrial effluents at levels that could threaten the sewerage system, treatment plant, public health, or the environment. 57. A withholding period is the time allowed for pathogen die-off between waste application and harvest. 58. The revised guidelines emphasize disease prevention and public health principles. They address the growing demand for guidance on the safe use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture. 59. The guidelines target environmental and public health scientists, researchers, engineers, policymakers, and those responsible for developing standards and regulations. 60. The guidelines are presented in four volumes: Volume 1 covers policy and regulatory aspects; Volume 2 addresses wastewater use in agriculture; Volume 3 focuses on wastewater and excreta use in aquaculture; and Volume 4 discusses excreta and greywater use in agriculture. 61. Volume 1 provides essential information for developing policies, procedures, and regulatory frameworks at national and local government levels. It also includes summaries of the other volumes in the series.
